bib.title: LoraHub: Efficient Cross-Task Generalization via Dynamic LoRA Composition

question: Can existing task-specific LoRA modules be composed automatically, using only a few examples of an unseen task and no gradients, to generalize across tasks?
hypothesis: LoRA modules are modular enough that a weighted element-wise combination, with weights found by gradient-free search on a handful of examples, can match few-shot in-context learning at much lower inference cost.
contributions: LoraHub: a framework with COMPOSE and ADAPT stages that assembles LoRA modules trained on upstream tasks for an unseen task from a few examples, with no extra parameters or gradients
Evaluation on BBH with FLAN-T5-large showing near-ICL average performance at zero-shot token cost, and a higher upper bound than ICL across demonstration sets
Release of code and pre-trained LoRA modules, with a vision of a LoRA sharing platform

method.summary: Train one LoRA module per upstream Flan task on FLAN-T5-large. For an unseen task, randomly pick 20 modules, combine them element-wise with scalar coefficients, and tune the coefficients with CMA-ES (via Nevergrad Shiwa) for 40 steps on 5 labelled examples, minimising cross-entropy plus an L1 penalty on the coefficients. The merged module is then fixed and used for inference.
method.task: few-shot cross-task generalization by composing LoRA modules (BBH multiple-choice tasks)

datasets.name: Flan Collection upstream tasks (LoRA training tasks)
datasets.size: nearly 200 distinct tasks; 20 modules sampled per experimental run

datasets.name: Big-Bench Hard (BBH)
datasets.size: 27 tasks (5 examples per task used for adaptation; test-set size not stated)

datasets.name: WikiTableQuestions (WTQ)
datasets.preprocessing: used for the check that a WTQ-trained LoRA added to the pool gets the highest weight

other.note: parameter count not stated in the text

training.objective: Candidate LoRA modules: per-task LoRA tuning (loss not named). LoraHub ADAPT: minimise cross-entropy L on the few-shot examples + alpha * sum_i |w_i|
training.optimizer: LoRA candidates: optimizer not stated. Coefficients w: gradient-free CMA-ES via Nevergrad (Shiwa selector), initialised at 0
training.lr: 1e-4 (candidate LoRA modules). Baselines: FFT 3e-5, IA3 and LoRA 2e-4
training.steps: K = 40 CMA-ES iterations per unseen task (ADAPT)
training.epochs: 10 (candidate LoRA modules); 40 (FFT, IA3, LoRA baselines on 5 examples)
training.regularisation: L1 on coefficients, alpha = 0.05; coefficients clipped so |w| <= 1.5
training.hardware: single A100 for adaptation in under a minute per BBH task; CPU-only feasible for LoraHub learning
training.compute: memory: FFT about 40GB, LoRA about 34GB, LoraHub about 5GB (LoRA-FA memory test settings)
training.wall_clock: less than a minute on one A100 per new BBH task (adaptation)
training.seeds: 3 runs with different 5-shot sets (main); 5 random seeds for FLAN-T5-xl and Fig 3 boxes

other.composition: m_hat = (sum w_i A_i)(sum w_i B_i); needs equal rank

inference.samples: 3 runs, each with different 5-shot examples; the average is reported (best also reported in Table 4)
inference.prompting: LoraHub and zero-shot: no demonstrations (111.6 tokens per example). ICL: the same 5 examples as demonstrations (597.8 tokens per example)

metrics.name: exact match (EM)
metrics.definition: exact match accuracy on BBH multiple-choice tasks, averaged over 27 tasks (Avg Performance Per Task)

metrics.name: Avg Tokens Per Example
metrics.definition: input tokens per example at inference

baselines: LoRA retrieval (best single module by few-shot loss)
eval.protocol: Mean over three runs with different 5-shot sets; gradient baselines are trained 40 epochs and tested at the end of training without model selection. No significance tests.

evidence.quote: In the case of FFT, a learning rate of 3e-5 is employed, whereas for IA3 and LoRA, we adopt a learning rate of 2e-4.
setting the batch size at 64, the learning rate at 1e −4, and the number of training epochs at 10

results.claim: Few-shot LoraHub on BBH averages 34.7 EM, above zero-shot (27.0) and below 5-shot ICL (37.3), at the zero-shot token count.
results.setup: FLAN-T5-large, 20 random LoRA candidates, 5 examples, K=40
results.table: Table 1, row Avg Performance Per Task, column LoraHub avg (34.7); Zero 27.0; ICL avg 37.3
results.note: Fig 1 shows 27.0, 37.5 and 34.7; Table 1 prints ICL avg as 37.3

results.claim: LoraHub uses the same tokens per example as zero-shot and far fewer than ICL.
results.table: Table 1, row Avg Tokens Per Example, columns LoraHub avg (111.6) and ICL avg (597.8)

results.claim: LoraHub beats IA3 by 3.1 points on average but trails LoRA tuning (37.7) and full fine-tuning (42.1).
results.setup: FLAN-T5-large, 40 epochs for gradient baselines on the same 5 examples
results.quote: our method exhibits a notable improvement of 3.1% on average in contrast to the promising IA3 method

results.claim: Best-of-three-runs LoraHub (41.2) exceeds best ICL (38.4) and, per the text, beats ICL on 18 tasks.
results.quote: the upper bound performance of our method across these runs can surpass ICL on 18 tasks
results.table: Table 4, row Best Performance (Average), columns LoraHub best (41.2), ICL best (38.4)
results.note: Selecting the best of three runs uses test performance, so it is an upper bound, not a deployable result

results.claim: Composition beats retrieving the single best LoRA by few-shot loss.
results.setup: FLAN-T5-large; modules ranked by loss on the few-shot examples, best one tested
results.table: Table 2, columns LoRA Retrieval (31.7), LoraHub avg (34.7), LoraHub best (41.2)

results.claim: LoraHub needs about 5GB of memory versus about 40GB for full fine-tuning and about 34GB for LoRA fine-tuning.
results.quote: LoraHub only utilized about 5GB of memory

results.claim: With FLAN-T5-xl, LoraHub averages 36.5 versus 25.8 zero-shot (best run 41.3).
results.setup: FLAN-T5-xl, 5 examples, average over 5 random seeds
results.table: Table 6, row Average Performance per Task, columns Zero (25.8), LoraHub avg (36.5), LoraHub best (41.3)

results.claim: On non-instruction-tuned T5-large, LoraHub reaches 20.78 average (rank 16) from near-zero zero-shot; rank 16 beats ranks 4 and 64.
results.table: Table 5, row Average Performance per Task, column 16avg (20.78)

results.claim: Pre-filtering to the 20 lowest-loss candidates gives a small gain, 35.4 versus 34.7.
results.table: Table 7, row Avg Performance Per Task, column LoraHub filter (35.4)

results.claim: Removing the coefficient bound drops average performance from 34.7 to 33.5 (about 1.2), mostly via three tasks.
results.quote: The resulting performance decline led to an average decrease of 1.2% compared to the setting with threshold.
results.note: Table 9 shows the threshold-free average as 33.5

results.claim: The top five influential upstream modules are mostly reading-comprehension and reasoning tasks; only RACE Is this the Right Answer gives a clear gain over FLAN-T5-large (+3.78).
results.setup: single module applied alone; Table 3 weights 0.72, 0.68, 0.63, 0.61, 0.58

results.claim: More candidate modules raise variance and the maximum achievable score, and most variance comes from which candidates are picked, not the optimizer seed.
results.setup: Figure 3, 15 BBH tasks, 5, 10, 50 and 100 modules, 5 runs per box
results.quote: once the candidates are determined, random seeds have minimal impact on the final performance

limits: LoraHub trails LoRA tuning and full fine-tuning, especially on tasks far from the upstream tasks (Dyck Languages: LoraHub and ICL about 1.0 while LoRA and FFT do well with 5 examples).
ADAPT costs extra inference steps (40 in the experiments); the authors say ICL is more pragmatic for one-time ad-hoc tasks, and LoraHub suits recurring tasks.
Performance is unstable with respect to which modules are randomly chosen; variance grows with the number of candidates, and the authors only add random selection or simple loss-based pre-filtering.
Everything is on BBH, mainly FLAN-T5-large, with candidate modules trained on the Flan tasks that FLAN-T5 was itself instruction-tuned on. No decoder-only LLMs are tested.
The 'upper bound beats ICL' claim takes the best of three runs on test data.
Modules must share base model and rank.
The reproducibility statement says code would be released on acceptance; the abstract gives the repository URLs.
Parameter count, candidate-LoRA optimizer, decoding settings and BBH test size are not stated in the text.

terms.definition: Few-shot adaptation to an unseen task by composing LoRA modules (COMPOSE) and tuning the coefficients with a gradient-free method (ADAPT).
Element-wise combination of LoRA modules with scalar coefficients w_i: m_hat = (w1A1 + ... + wNAN)(w1B1 + ... + wNBN)
Updating w with a gradient-free algorithm to reduce loss on the few-shot examples Q
